Explosion hits another EMCO weapons site in Bulgaria; probe underway
description: SOFIA, Sept 12 () - Bulgaria is investigating the cause of a fire at a weapons storage facility operated by EMCO, including the possibility of sabotage and a link to a previous blaze at ‌another of th...
fullText:
SOFIA, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Bulgaria is investigating the cause of a fire at a weapons storage facility operated by EMCO, including the possibility of sabotage and a link to a previous blaze at ‌another of the company's facilities in August, the interior minister said.

No injuries were reported in the fire, ‌which broke out near the village of Tsareva Livada and lit up the night sky, according to videos broadcast locally. The incident came weeks after ​an explosion and fire at another EMCO weapons depot in western Bulgaria.

Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev told journalists on Saturday that the fire was under control and that an investigation was underway.

"We will review previous cases in which similar fires occurred in the warehouses of this company, as well as at other companies, in order to look for a possible connection or a ‌similar pattern," he said.

"We are not ruling ⁠out outside interference."

EMCO later said in a statement that the fire was the result of sabotage, citing more than 10 similar incidents at Bulgarian defence firms since 2011, although it ⁠did not identify any suspects.

"There is no reason to assume that this case is any different," the company said.

EMCO is run by Bulgarian arms trader Emilian Gebrev, who Bulgarian prosecutors have previously alleged was the target of attacks on his facilities by Russian ​operatives.

In 2024, ​Bulgaria issued arrest warrants for six Russian citizens accused of ​involvement in the destruction of EMCO arms depots ‌that stored munitions destined for export to Ukraine and Georgia between 2011 and 2020.

Prosecutors at the time said they had grounds to suspect links between the blasts in Bulgaria, an attempted poisoning of Gebrev in 2015, and munitions depot explosions in the Czech Republic in 2014.

Moscow has dismissed the allegations.

Slavcho Dimiev, manager of EMCO's production facilities, confirmed Saturday's fire at the storage site, which he said mainly holds ammunition, including a small quantity of medium-calibre rounds.

The company also accused authorities ‌of failing to adequately protect defence facilities.

"Not a single investigation into ​the more than ten such incidents at the industry's leading enterprises ​has been concluded," the company said, adding that its ​warehouse has been inspected seven times since the beginning of the year, with the last one ‌20 days prior.

Demerdzhiev expressed concerns about the security ​and the conditions under which ​explosives are stored and the way these facilities are guarded.

The blast comes at a time of flux in Bulgarian politics after Prime Minister Rumen Radev came to power in April on a Kremlin-friendly ticket.But in June, the ​newly appointed defence minister, Dimitar Stoyanov, said ‌Bulgaria would no longer provide arms to Ukraine and urged Moscow and Kyiv to sit down at ​the negotiating table to end the war.

title: Kamala Harris claims GOP 'cheating' ahead of midterms, says she's focused on stopping the 'madness'
description: Former Vice President Kamala Harris accused Republicans of "cheating" by redrawing lines and suppressing votes, telling Megan Rapinoe she's focused on winning midterms.
fullText:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris accused Republicans of "cheating" during an interview Thursday and said she was working to "stop the madness" by helping Democrats win the midterm elections.

"Midterms, midterms, midterms, full-time occupying my thoughts, my mind and my work," Harris said.

"We have to win these midterms. These — these folks are cheating. They're redrawing lines. They're trying to make it more difficult for people to vote so they won't vote because they are afraid of the power of the people.

"And, so, I'm spending full-time working on doing everything I can to help people restore some balance in our government, which is, through the midterms, winning back Congress, the House and the Senate so that we can stop the madness," Harris told former women's soccer star Megan Rapinoe on her podcast, "What Are You Like?"

Kamala Harris Dives Into Midterm Fight Only To Get Roasted For Never Having 'An Original Thought In Her Life'

Rapinoe asked Harris about what brought her back into political and public life.

"I don't know how to live and not serve. I honestly don't. I just don't. It's something I've come to terms with. I don't know how to, I just don't know a life without figuring out how I can help move the needle," she said.

Harris said she wanted to restore "some sense of sanity" and a functioning government.

"If Kamala Harris is upset Republicans are going after the illegals and fraudsters trying to vote, it makes you wonder if she's taking crazy pills again. Voter ID and proof of citizenship are common sense, but Democrats can't win elections without cheating the system," RNC election integrity Communications Director Ally Triolo told Fox News Digital in a statement.

Fox News Poll: Significant Support For Both Voter Id Laws And Mail-in Ballots

Rapinoe also asked the former vice president if she had made a decision about running in 2028.

"I haven't decided," Harris said. "From my perspective, '28 doesn't matter if we don't win '26."

Harris said during an interview last week with MS NOW's Peter Alexander that she even supported Democrats who don't want her on the campaign trail with them, because, she said, they need to do whatever it takes to win.

"Listen, Peter, we need to win, OK? Bottom line, we need to win," Harris said. "I have run locally, I've run for statewide office and, obviously, nationally. And these candidates know what they need to do to win, and I would expect nothing less.

"I look forward to being on the trail and helping folks where I can be helpful, but we have got to put a check on this lawless administration and deliver what Americans need and deserve. Lower costs, affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, you name it. So, I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win."

Kamala Harris Backs Major Changes To The Supreme Court, Electoral College Ahead Of Possible 2028 Campaign

Rapinoe also discussed her experience as a female athlete.

"I'm thinking about my own experience being a female athlete, and I went through, in the prime of my career, just the most historic time in women's sports," she said. "I mean, it was crazy in the best ways. We saw a huge amount of progress, which has led into a pretty significant regression in terms of just equal rights and people's rights in general. I definitely think those two are tied.

"It was for the longest time, you know, don't talk about women's issues," she added. "Same kind of thing. It was like, 'Well, you're not that good,' or 'You're not that entertaining' or, 'Don't do it like this or whatever.'

"And then we did it, and all women's sports sort of did it. And then it was like, 'OK, we're just going to do something else.' And I always just felt like they're like they're not going to let us just win."

title: Norris takes Madrid pole with 'gorgeous' lap
description: Lando Norris takes a superb pole position for McLaren at the Spanish Grand Prix, beating Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen.
fullText:
Lando Norris took a superb pole position for McLaren at the Spanish Grand Prix, beating Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and Red Bull's Max Verstappen in a breathless final few seconds of qualifying.

"Oh, what a lap, gorgeous," said an ecstatic Norris after pipping world championship leader Antonelli by just 0.011 seconds. "Oh, that might be my best one."

Verstappen was 0.140secs off the pace, as all three moved ahead of Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari in Madrid.

The seven-time champion had held the top spot after the first runs in the final session.

Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc was fifth, ahead of Mercedes' George Russell and the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

Norris' pole came from nowhere. He had been fifth in the first session of qualifying, seventh in the second, and 0.449secs slower than Hamilton's pace-setting lap after the first runs in the final session.

How to follow Spanish Grand Prix on the BBC

The world champion said: "I'm shocked. I'm a little bit surprised to be here. It was probably one of the best laps I've done ever in my career.

"One of those laps when everything came together. I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, it was whether it came together but my brain let me do it almost perfect. It's one of those laps when you look at the time and go: 'Oh, that was pretty good."

The session had started with predictions of a crash-fest, after drivers had been warning about the high-risk nature of the new Madring street circuit, with tricky entries to corners and walls coming back at the drivers on the exits.

Two red flags during final practice had led some teams to have private sweepstakes as to how many stoppages there would be in qualifying, but the session ran cleanly, with no incidents.

Pole looked to be a battle between Antonelli and the Ferraris, with Verstappen perhaps in the mix.

In the end, the Ferraris faded, as they so often have this year when it really matters, and Norris rose to the front with a breathtaking performance.

"The adrenaline was high on the last lap," he said. "You have to relax and let it all flow.

"It's easy to get tense around here. There's a lot of walls that come at you pretty quickly. I have been feeling pretty good, I just wasn't relaxed.

"I was pretty much perfect apart from the last corner, where I thought I was in the wall. Everything I wanted to achieve I achieved and it's one of those moments when I was in that flow state."

Hamilton, who had crashed at the final corner in practice and missed the final half of the session, did improve on his last lap, but only by 0.06secs and it was not enough to prevent him falling backwards.

He edged Leclerc by just 0.006secs as Ferrari rued yet another tantalising chance slipping through their fingers.

Hamilton said: "I felt pretty awesome in Q3 run one, and then just didn't have any more grip or power in the last one."

Norris' performance was put in perspective by Piastri, who was 0.470secs off his team-mate's pace.

Russell, meanwhile, could have done with a morale-boosting performance after he finished second to Antonelli in Monza last weekend when the Italian took a stunning win from 19th on the grid.

The Briton had looked more or less on Antonelli's pace for much of the weekend, even if he clearly lacked the Italian's fluid ability to let the car run free and flow and slide on corner exits.

And in qualifying the difference was a stark 0.314secs, increasing the prospect of the 66-point gap in the championship between them extending still further on Sunday.

Russell said: "I was in the mix to fight for pole and that last lap of Q3, I just really pushed the limit, was about 0.3secs up and then lost it all towards the end of the lap with the tyres overheating, so that was quite a shame.

"As the track has got faster, I have just been struggling to get the most out of the tyres, I have just been sliding rather than going around the corners faster and I need to understand why that is."

The top 10 was completed by Red Bull's Liam Lawson, Alpine's Franco Colapinto and the Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad, the British rookie again impressing.

Local heroes Carlos Sainz and Fernando Alonso were unable to give the Spanish fans much to cheer about as both were knocked out after the first session in 17th and 18th places.

It got worse for Williams' Sainz because stewards later imposed a three-place grid penalty for impeding Cadillac's Valtteri Bottas, meaning he will start in 20th.

title: Why Canada? America's northern neighbor seems an unlikely target for a trade war
description: Canada might seem an unlikely target for a U.S. trade war.  For American farmers, Canada is second only to Mexico as an export market.  A North American trade pact — negotiated by President Donald Trump during his first term — means that most American products enter Canada duty-free.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Canada might seem an unlikely target for a U.S. trade war.

No country on Earth buys as much from the United States as its northern neighbor. For American farmers, Canada is second only to Mexico as an export market.

A North American trade pact — negotiated by President Donald Trump during his first term — means that most American products enter Canada duty-free. Rankings of the world's most open economies usually put Canada near the top.

But when Trump looks at Canada, he says, he sees a predator out to cheat the United States and strangle its industries.

America has been "ripped off for 50 years by Canada," the president declared Saturday when asked if he was considering pulling out of the three-way agreement he signed with the leaders of Canada and Mexico in late 2018.

Relations between the U.S. and Canada have deteriorated since their latest trade talks collapsed Aug. 21. Trump has goaded Canada's leaders with personal attacks and portrayed the longtime U.S. ally as weak. After alienating the Canadian public last year by repeatedly floating the idea of making Canada the 51st state, he signed an executive order last month directing the federal government to change Lake Ontario's name to "Lake America."

Each side blamed the other for the failed negotiations. Trump slapped 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian products three weeks ago to protest what he described as discrimination against U.S. auto, dairy and alcoholic beverage exports.

When Canada's government retaliated Tuesday with tariffs of its own, the president moved to ban imports of the dairy byproduct whey, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles and mopeds from Canada, though he said several products, including toilet paper, bedsheets and fishing rods, would be removed as tariff targets.

Landing on the list of nations with allegedly unfair trade policies is a jarring turn of events for Canada, a country that built its economy around international commerce. Canada's trade is equal to 64% of its economic output, the World Bank says, versus 25% for America.

The conservative Heritage Foundation in Washington ranked Canada No. 14 (out of 184 economies) on its Index of Economic Freedom; the United States landed eight spots lower at No. 22. The libertarian Fraser Institute in Vancouver likewise ranked Canada No. 11 (out of 165 countries and territories) on its Economic Freedom of the World report.

Before the latest blowup, Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the United States imposed on Canada, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Most U.S. exports enter Canada duty-free under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement that took effect on July 1, 2020.

title: Ruthless Canada outclass Scotland in WXV opener
description: Canada prove too strong for Scotland as they score 10 tries to register a resounding win in their WXV Series opener in Edinburgh.
fullText:
Tries: Gallagher, Campbell, Skeldon, Lloyd Cons: Nelson 3

Tries: Gibson 2, Apps 2, Kassil, Omokhuale, Perry, Pelletier, Senft, Bauder Cons: Gallagher 7

World Cup finalists Canada proved too strong for Scotland as they ran in 10 tries to register a resounding win in their WXV Series opener in Edinburgh.

Canada struck early when a brilliant offload from hooker Kiki Idowu found Rachel Smith on the charge and left the Scottish defence scrambling.

The 2025 World Cup runners-up held out for multiple phases on their own line before Lizzie Gibson found the gap to dive over for the opening try.

They quickly scored a second when scrum-half Olivia Apps darted over in the corner.

Scotland needed a response and they got it when Evie Gallagher – on her first Test appearance since last year's World Cup - blasted over from close range to bring the hosts back within five points.

The response was swift, however, as Gibson sliced through for her second try to re-establish Canada's 12-points lead.

Brittanny Kassil – who would receive a 20-minute red card after the break for a high shot on Meryl Smith - and Julia Omokhuale blasted over from close range for two tries in quick succession as the Canadians started to flex their muscles.

The Scots gave the home crowd something to cheer with their second try.

Debutant Rhea Clarke did brilliantly to strip opposite number Apps in contact. She set Gallagher free and she held off two tackles before finding Shona Campbell on her shoulder to score.

Fly-half Taylor Perry extinguished any hopes of a Scottish fightback as she sliced through the midfield untouched for Canada's sixth try early in the second half.

The Scots were tiring and Apps carved them open with a lovely little show-and-go to streak away and go in under the sticks.

Hooker Lana Skeldon burrowed over for Scotland's third try, but substitute Justine Pelletier responded in kind almost immediately.

Helen Nelson dinked a wonderful little kick over the Canada defence and into the arms of Rhona Lloyd to go over for Scotland's fourth, but Gabrielle Senft powered over and substitute Savannah Bauder scored a fabulous individual try on her Test debut to ensure Canada had the last word.

The Scots face New Zealand at Hive Stadium next Saturday (17:10 BST), while Canada face England at Sandy Park in a re-run of last year's World Cup final on the same day (15:00).

title: Osborne makes history as first female jockey to win British Classic
description: Saffie Osborne becomes the first female jockey to win a British Classic Flat race, claiming victory in the St Leger on Highwayman.
fullText:
Saffie Osborne has become the first female jockey to win one of British Flat racing's five Classics, riding Highwayman to victory in the St Leger at Doncaster.

The 24-year-old burst clear of the field on the 11-1 chance in the closing stages to create history in the 250th anniversary of the world's oldest Classic Flat race.

It was a one-two for winning trainer Joseph O'Brien, whose colt Enceladus (5-2) finished second, two-and-a-half lengths back.

Aidan O'Brien was bidding to become just the third trainer to win a fourth consecutive St Leger but had to be content with third with Amelia Earhart (22-1).

Pre-race favourite Christmas Day (7-4) was heavily backed to give Aidan O'Brien that historic fourth victory in a row and complete the Derby-St Leger double, but finished well down in ninth place.

"I definitely didn't have this on the bingo card this week," Osborne told ITV Sport immediately after the historic victory in the fifth and final Classic of the British Flat season.

"I didn't even know if I would be riding the St Leger on Monday morning."

No female jockey has won any of the other four Classics - the 1,000 Guineas and 2,000 Guineas at Newmarket and the Oaks and Derby at Epsom.

Osborne was quick to thank the trainer for giving her the ride, adding: "I have to thank Joseph and his team for putting their faith in me. It won't change Joseph's life, but it's changed mine."

The jockey is the daughter of trainer and former top National Hunt jockey Jamie Osborne, while her mother, Katie O'Sullivan, is a highly-regarded equine artist.

She started as an apprentice in 2020 and finished second in the apprentice championship the following season.

Osborne went on to be crowned leading jockey in the Racing League for three consecutive seasons from 2022 to 2024.

In 2024, she became the first female jockey to win a race at the Dubai Carnival, on Ouzo, while her first Classic ride came in the same season, finishing eighth on Ed Walker's Ten Bob Tony in the 2,000 Guineas.

Like Rachel Blackmore, the first female jockey to win the Grand National, her name will now go down in racing folklore.

Joseph O'Brien was at Leopardstown for the Irish Champion Stakes on Saturday, but delighted Highwayman owner John Neocleous was at Doncaster to share the moment with Osborne.

"Saffie is amazing, I'm sure she's in shock as well," he said after watching her storm clear at the end of the one mile six furlong trip.

"Joseph came up with the idea, but he called me first and I was extremely happy to have her. She's an up-and-coming jockey, she knows how to ride a finish and I thought if she rode a good finish maybe we'd be placed.

"But she won comprehensively so I'm very happy. I said to Saffie, 'let's go and make history', but I didn't really believe it!"

The surprise victory continues trainer Joseph O'Brien's love affair with the St Leger.

He won the race as a jockey on Leading Light in 2013 and claimed his first victory as a trainer in 2020 with Galileo Chrome.

Enceladus was expected to be his best chance to double his number of winners in the famous old race, having hit top form this season with three big victories, including in the Gordon Stakes at Goodwood.

But Highwayman had also showed rapid improvement this year, especially in winning the Vinnie Roe Stakes at Leopardstown.

title: GB's Hewett beats Oda to win fifth US Open title
description: Great Britain's Alfie Hewett beats Japanese top seed Tokito Oda to win a fifth US Open title and his 11th Grand Slam singles crown overall.
fullText:
Britain's Alfie Hewett beat Tokito Oda to clinch a fifth US Open men's wheelchair singles title and prevent the Japanese top seed from completing a clean sweep at the Grand Slams in 2026.

A 6-0 7-6 (7-5) victory meant Hewett added to the doubles title he won alongside fellow Briton Gordon Reid on Friday.

Hewett, 28, lost to Oda in the finals of the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this year, winning only two games in a 6-1 6-1 defeat at SW19, while the Japanese also triumphed at January's Australian Open.

Hewett told BBC Sport that his loss to Oda at Wimbledon made him "look in the mirror" and a period of reflection led to him wanting to "be a little bit more like me" as he pursued an 11th Grand Slam singles title.

"I'm known for being just as fearless, brave and courageous in big moments and I felt I was everything but that in Wimbledon," Hewett said.

"I was quiet, I was timid, I was a shell of myself.

"I think I have had six weeks of champing at the bit to come out and prove to myself that I can be more like that person."

Hewett described his first-set performance as "possessed" as, after saving a break point in the opening game, he produced a dominant display, clinching the opener with a superb backhand return winner.

The Briton secured victory in a second-set tie-break, having fought back from a double break down and saved three set points for Oda to level the match.

Oda, who had won the past six Grand Slam singles titles, said on court: "Definitely I was trying to get the calendar year [Grand Slam] this year.

"This was the last part of it so it's really tough for me, but I think Alfie deserved it today."

GB's Skupski wins US Open doubles title with Harrison

title: 'I'm still in shock' - GB's Skupski wins US Open doubles title with Harrison
description: Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison win the US Open men's doubles to secure their second Grand Slam title together.
fullText:
Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison won the US Open men's doubles title to claim their second Grand Slam trophy together.

The fifth seeds did not drop a set in New York as they beat sixth seeds Tim Puetz and Kevin Krawietz 6-4 7-6 (8-6) to secure the title.

Victory adds to Skupski and Harrison's Australian Open triumph in January in what was their first Grand Slam as a pairing.

Skupski had suffered a heartbreaking defeat in last year's US Open final, missing three championship points when he reached the showpiece alongside fellow Briton Joe Salisbury.

He and Dutchman Wesley Koolhof were also beaten in the 2022 final.

Salisbury later took a break from tennis because of anxiety, which led to Skupski partnering up with Harrison.

Cheered by the Flushing Meadows crowd, who rallied behind home hope Harrison, the pair saved a set point in the second set tie-break before Skupski sealed victory with a smash at the net.

"I don't know what to say really, I'm still in shock. The speech gets a little bit easier once you've won," said Skupski.

"Losing twice and having championship points in the final last year was a tough part of my career, but it's amazing what a year does in tennis."

Skupski and Harrison secured the first and only break of the match in the first set, the American slamming a backhand winner down the line to lead 4-3 before seeing out the opener.

The second set remained on serve until the tie-break, where Puetz and Krawietz profited from a return which clipped the net and wrong-footed Harrison to give the Germans a set point.

Skupski and Harrison saved it and then brought up championship point as the noise levels rose on Arthur Ashe Stadium.

Skupski dropped to his knees in celebration after sealing victory before turning to hug Harrison.

Victory at Flushing Meadows marks Skupski's third doubles Grand Slam title after he won at Wimbledon in 2023 alongside Koolhof.

Skupski also has two mixed doubles Grand Slam titles to his name after winning Wimbledon in 2021 and 2022 with American Desirae Krawczyk.

title: 'Absolute joke' to be worried - Mitchell on England's response
description: England produce dominant second-half performance to comfortably defeat Australia at CorpAcq Stadium in the opening game of the new WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Tries: Burton, Campbell, Jones, Field, Venner, Kabeya, L Packer, Moloney-MacDonald Cons: Aitchison, Harrison 3

Tries: Pohiva, Karpani Con: Wood Pen: Wood

England produced a dominant second-half performance to defeat Australia at CorpAcq Stadium in the opening game of the new WXV Global Series.

The world champions, playing their first game since winning a record eighth successive Women's Six Nations title in May, were made to work for victory in Salford after trailing at half-time for the first time since 2020.

The Wallaroos led 10-5 at the break, with player of the match Abi Burton scoring England's only try in an error-strewn first half.

John Mitchell's side responded emphatically after the interval, scoring seven tries to quickly put any prospect of a shock defeat to bed and extend their record winning run to 39 matches in front of a crowd of 9,251.

The England head coach described the fixture as "a good pre-season game" after it kicked off the 2026-27 campaign for his players.

"It was the first pre-season game of the year where we had the reality of playing rugby and had to solve [problems], which is good for us," Mitchell told BBC Sport.

"It is an absolute joke if you are worried about being down 10-5. More important is how we worked our way back into it.

"We got 23 players with rugby [into them], and it was a 43-point second half."

During a dominant 20-minute spell, May Campbell, captain Meg Jones, Bryony Field, Mia Venner and Sadia Kabeya all crossed for tries.

Lucy Packer and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald also then scored, with Australia's Asoiva Karpani adding to Faliki Pohiva's first-half try.

The WXV Global Series has replaced the WXV competition, with England having won both editions of the premier section, WXV1, in 2023 and 2024.

Running from 2026 to 2028, the series features the world's top 12 teams and is designed to provide more competitive matches before the 2029 World Cup in Australia.

The Red Roses face Canada at Exeter's Sandy Park next weekend, the teams' first meeting since England won last year's Rugby World Cup final, before facing New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on 26 September.

"They're great rivals [Canada], a fantastic rugby team, well-coached, a different team to Australia," Mitchell added.

"We only have a very short turnaround. With this being our first pre-season game, lots of players got rugby, so we'll be in a great place."

England blitz Australia in second half to maintain winning run - reaction & try clips

This was the first game with the new women's size 4.5 ball, which is 3% smaller than the standard size five.

In May, England fly-half Zoe Harrison, arguably the best goal-kicker in the women's game, said introducing the ball was "the worst decision someone has ever made".

Scrum-half Samantha Wood confidently drilled over an early penalty as Australia, like they did against England in Brighton in last year's World Cup, started quicker.

Sloppy handling and inaccuracy in the Wallaroos' 22 held back Mitchell's side in the first half.

Burton's try came from slick handling and interplay, indicating what new attack coach Emily Scarratt is trying to implement, even if England were not at their brightest early on.

"The message at half-time was we know that we weren't at our best, so we knew we needed to come out and rip back into them and give it to them physically because they came out absolutely gunning," Burton told BBC Sport.

"At the end that cohesiveness started to kick in.

"There's so much more to come from this team, just a few teething issues we needed to sort out."

Both sides had tries disallowed in the first half, but Australia scrambled brilliantly in defence to take a deserved lead into the break.

The Red Roses have often started slowly under Mitchell before clicking into gear, with the power of their bench a level above the rest.

However, England had not trailed at half-time since a match against France in November 2020.

Mitchell said that, without a "tournament to win", his side have to be "very patient" in how they approach these Test matches.

With a shock defeat potentially looming, his side turned to their destructive maul to power over the line before a scrum penalty gave them valuable field position.

A clever grubber kick from Sale Sharks' Holly Aitchison, on her 50th cap, then found Jones as the combination of power and backline skill finally came together.

When in need of a try, the Red Roses maul tends to deliver more often than not.

It was England's pack that dominated Canada to win the World Cup, and it delivered again through Field to give them some breathing room.

England, with the likes of Hannah Botterman and Marlie Packer coming off the bench, continued to grow into the game as their accuracy improved while Australia tired.

Both wingers crossed to underline the balance in play that has made Mitchell's side so difficult to beat.

Harrison also nailed three conversions, underlining a successful adjustment to the new ball.

Both Canada and New Zealand will pose more of a threat in attack and will take note of how Australia made life difficult for the Red Roses in the first half.

But it is yet another win for a side who, simply put, seem to know little else.

title: Was Hull-Woad pairing right call as Europe & US end level with singles to play?
description: Should Europe fail to reach the 14½ points they require to win the Solheim Cup on Sunday questions will surely be asked of captain Anna Nordqvist's faith in Charley Hull and Lottie Woad as a pairing.
fullText:
Should Europe fail to reach the 14½ points they require to win the Solheim Cup on Sunday, questions will surely be asked of captain Anna Nordqvist's faith in Charley Hull and Lottie Woad as a pairing.

Europe's misfiring star pair were beaten in both of Saturday's sessions and have contributed just half a point from four matches to the scoreline of 8-8 as the contest heads into Sunday's decisive 12 singles matches.

Woad confirmed on Saturday evening that "Plan A" had always revolved around her and Hull featuring in all five matches, but with their struggles particularly evident on the greens it begs the question of why that strategy was not revisited.

"We didn't hole many putts in the morning and all afternoon, and that's the difference, really," Woad said.

"The people we played were holing 15-footers and we weren't."

"Just couldn't buy a putt," was Hull's summation of the day before Woad added: "It doesn't matter who wins the points. I would happily lose my matches if we win."

But while there were few plaudits for the English duo, the irrepressible Swedish pairing of Maja Stark and Linn Grant led the charge for Nordqvist's team at Bernardus Golf Club in the Netherlands.

Having defeated the unbeaten US partnership of world number one Nelly Korda and Allisen Corpuz 3&2 in the morning foursomes, Stark and Grant fought back in wonderful fashion to triumph 2&1 against Megan Khang and the previously undefeated Lauren Coughlin in the afternoon fourballs.

Starting day two level at 2-2, the Swede's opening point, against a Korda and Corpuz pairing that had won all five of their previous matches together, set the tone for Europe to win three points.

Mimi Rhodes and Nastasia Nadaud became the first rookie duo to win two matches in one edition of the biggest team competition in women's golf, while Leona Maguire and Esther Henseleit also delivered a point as Europe led 7-5.

Stark and Grant were sent out in the afternoon and delivered a third point of the week to maintain their 100% record at this year's event.

It was Khang's first loss for six matches and it delivered a wonderful boost to Nordqvist's team as the US challenge warmed up in the afternoon and threatened to overturn Europe's advantage.

However, Nordqvist's decision to persist with Hull and Woad will surely be placed under further scrutiny given the way events unfolded.

The pair, Europe's highest ranked players, had asked to play together this week.

But after they were summarily thrashed by Alison Lee and Coughlin in the foursomes – a Solheim Cup record equalling 6&5 defeat – the experiment of pairing the world number seven and eight together looked to have run its course.

Yet when Hull and Woad emerged together again to face Yealimi Noh and Andrea Lee, to almost universal surprise, Europe's captain defended her decision.

"I don't think people understand - these are the best players in the world," said a defiant Nordqvist.

"Lottie, herself, made six birdies in the afternoon [yesterday]. They are playing solid."

Unfortunately solid was not enough to prevail in the fourballs, particularly with Noh delivering a performance that included five birdies and an eagle on the front nine.

A Woad birdie on the 17th sent the match down the last with the English pair needing to win the hole to salvage half a point.

But for the second day running, Hull found water off the tee to immediately put pressure on Woad and Noh and Lee held on for the win.

Woad also pointed out that their opponents in Friday's fourball and Saturday's foursomes matches just played better golf.

"In the fourball, we were 10, 11 under, and it was a great match," said the European rookie.

"And then I don't think anyone would have beaten who we played on Saturday morning. They were seven under through 14, so credit to them.

"Everyone's played amazing when we've played them. So, yeah, it's just matchplay, isn't it? You can play bad and win and play well and lose."

And the day ended with a huge momentum swing for the US.

Jennifer Kupcho holed a monster 91-foot putt on the 17th and followed it by dispatching another lengthy putt on the final hole to steal an unlikely point from the grasp of Carlota Ciganda and Celine Boutier who had been one up with four to play.

Just as Ciganda pilfered a half point in Friday's final match to give Europe the impetus coming into Saturday, so Kupcho's point will do likewise for the US, who need to reach 14 points on Sunday to retain the trophy.

title: New system, same problems - Alonso not happy with 'soft' Chelsea
description: It was subdued at Stamford Bridge after Chelsea's 2-2 draw with newly promoted Hull City.
fullText:
It was a familiar story for the Premier League's top scorers.

Chelsea's entertaining 2-2 draw with Hull on Saturday means the Blues have now found the net 10 times this season - but they have also conceded two or more goals in each of their opening four league matches for the first time in 11 years.

Only Crystal Palace and Ipswich Town have conceded more than Chelsea's nine goals in the top flight so far this season.

The issue predates manager Xabi Alonso's arrival. Chelsea are now without a clean sheet in 20 league matches stretching back to January, their longest such run for 65 years.

Alonso still appears to be experimenting. This week alone, he changed shape in three successive matches - from the defeat at Arsenal to the 6-3 Carabao Cup win over Leeds in midweek and again against Hull.

Yet it was Hull who looked more likely to find a winner. No wonder there was a subdued mood at Stamford Bridge.

Alonso summed up the feeling afterwards, saying his side needed to be "competing better" and avoid being "soft" in duels.

There were also individual errors.

Jorrel Hato misjudged a cross before Hull scored their equaliser, while Mohamed Belloumi's second goal came after Chelsea failed to clear a corner.

Despite an early goal from Morgan Rogers and a second-half equaliser from Joao Pedro, with Cole Palmer involved in both strikes, Chelsea had to settle for a point.

Hull boss Sergej Jakirovic even described Chelsea goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez as the "man of the match" after the Argentine denied Oli McBurnie, Mohamed-Ali Cho and Lucas Herrington.

Asked about Chelsea's defensive issues, former defender and BBC pundit Ashley Williams said: "Chelsea are all over the place in transitions. When they lose the ball, they are wide open. The goals they conceded are just basic errors.

"Both individually and as a defensive unit, they are so far off it and are shipping goals. They are not going to achieve what they want this season defending like that."

With Rogers, Palmer and Joao Pedro in fine form offensively this season, the Blues know they need to find solutions defensively.

Alonso said: "We had one or two good chances to get the winner, but you're still open. Not happy. We can do better. We got what we deserved.

"We need to be more solid and be more controlled. [We have] new players and new staff. This is the process. In a few months I'm sure we'll be able to control better."

However, he said his decision to switch to a back four was not a solution to recent defensive issues, explaining: "It's about the profile of the players.

"You can say it was back three or four, so it's about the choice of the players, their qualities, where they play better.

"Today we played with Malo [Gusto], he was playing in good positions, trying to find him and on the right linking with other players, so it wasn't that much of a change for me."

It was a "tactical" decision to take Hato off at half-time, he continued, before going into more detail about what it will take to fix Chelsea's issues.

"It's all maybe entertaining, but I hope that one day you say it was a boring game and we win and we don't give these entertaining moments," Alonso added. "But for sure it kind of repeats some patterns that we are making.

"It will take time or it will take moments to fix them when we get the lead and you still need to be competing and not to give the chance so easily for them to come back. Especially in the first goal, we can do much better.

"It was too soft to give them this hope because until then we were controlling, we were creating chances, but that momentum that we had changed the mood and the score of the game and it's something that we need to be talking [about], we address and we will get better, but it's having an impact on our performances at the moment."

There will be concerns going into the trip to Brentford on Friday, the last match before the three-week international break, given that the Bees are known to be dangerous at set-pieces.

It's not just set-pieces, though. Chelsea have conceded the majority of the goals from open play, which is something Alonso acknowledged.

"Overall, I think that we are attacking better than defending in every part," he continued.

"We know that it's a big topic and a big theme for us. For sure it's just four games, but the dynamic in terms of conceding, I don't like it and we need to do much better. Open play, set-pieces, long balls, this toughness, this competitive sense, we can do better."

Some players, like Malo Gusto, have been criticised by supporters, and his substitution was celebrated by his own fans inside Stamford Bridge.

Meanwhile, with Moises Caicedo out injured, Chelsea have looked short of quality and numbers in the middle of the park.

Monaco pulled the plug on Chelsea's £47m deal to sign midfielder Lamine Camara on deadline day, having made attempts to sign Roma's Manu Kone and Fulham's Sander Berge as alternative options.

Key defensive signing Maxence Lacroix was left out on Saturday but none of the defensive options have excelled this season, although their attack remain in blistering form.

It will be on Alonso to fix these problems on the training pitch with no more opportunities to sign players until the January transfer window.

title: Norris' real opportunity after coming from nowhere with 'masterpiece' lap
description: McLaren do not have the fastest car at the Spanish Grand Prix but with overtaking expected to be difficult, pole man Lando Norris has a chance of another win.
fullText:
It says everything about the remarkable lap with which Lando Norris took pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix that it was a toss-up as to which was the most important and impressive of two striking statistics.

Was it that Norris had improved by a stunning 0.701 seconds between his two laps in final qualifying, to come from nowhere to take a pole that had not looked to be a possibility to McLaren?

Or was it that in beating runaway championship leader Kimi Antonelli's Mercedes by 0.011 seconds, Norris had made a mistake at the final corner that cost him more than 0.3secs?

McLaren team principal Andrea Stella described Norris' performance as "a masterpiece" and "one of the most impressive laps that I witnessed as somebody that watches telemetry in 450 grands prix, because we were not honestly performing to the level of scoring pole position".

As Stella is someone who has worked with Michael Schumacher and Fernando Alonso, his comments carry weight.

Norris takes Madrid pole with 'gorgeous' lap

How to follow Spanish Grand Prix on the BBC

Norris said: "Most tracks, you know what is perfect, what you really want to achieve in a perfect lap. A very good day is when you get pretty close to that.

"Until the last corner, I think I matched that perfection level in pretty much every corner.

"So, yeah, it's a dream to achieve a lap like that. So it was easily one of the best laps I've ever done.

"Everything came together perfectly. I got the timing of everything so dialled in, with the kerb hits, how you hit the kerb, brake points, all of these things. It's so easy to make a mistake on a day like today and a track like this, but really I just got it right on the most important lap I had to do.

"So, very excited, very pleased and it's not often you achieve a lap like today and it's a pretty awesome feeling when you do."

That last corner, Norris said, "I thought I was in the wall and that was just from over-pushing. I got a bit excited in the car and I just over-pushed the entry."

Stella said: "The most impressive thing is the fact that it's a pole position despite having lost 0.35secs in the last corner, which means that it would have been a pretty convincing pole position without this issue.

"The thing that makes the lap unique when you look especially at the telemetry is the precision - the braking, the speed you carry in entry, the striking of the kerbs, the going on power. Everything is executed with a pretty unique level of precision."

Norris does not use a display on his dashboard showing his progress compared with his previous lap, the so-called delta, as most other drivers do.

"I don't need my delta," he said. "I can feel when I do what I need to do and when I get a good exit, when I'm on the limit of things. When I'm kind of a bit uncomfortable in corners is normally when it's going pretty well. So, I could feel it and I feel like I just made all the right things. My feet were doing what I wanted, and that's normally when things are going well."

The new Madring street circuit is in an unprepossessing location, snaking around an exhibition centre near the Spanish capital's international airport, about a 15-minute drive from the city with no traffic.

But as a test for the drivers, it is right up there.

"Very high risk" and "less margin than Monaco" were two remarks made by Mercedes driver George Russell over the weekend.

The walls are close and the demands of the circuit are amplified by the fact that the barriers angle back towards the track on the exit of many corners, making it all too easy to hit them.

Despite that, qualifying ran incident-free, which was very much not the prediction, especially after there were two red flags in final practice earlier in the day, one caused by seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton, the other by Haas driver Oliver Bearman.

Whether the race goes the same way is an altogether different matter.

This was Norris' third pole of the year, and after the first two he took dominant wins in Hungary and the Netherlands.

At those races, though, McLaren were in a very different place.

"Tomorrow is going to be a very tough day," Norris said. "It's not going to be as straightforward as in Zandvoort and Budapest. There we were the quickest car. Yes, I'm on pole now, but we're not in the quickest car. It took a perfect lap to get me on pole by 0.011secs today."

Norris, it's worth saying, also took pole despite missing virtually all of second practice with a gearbox problem.

Not only does that make the achievement all the more impressive, it also means he missed out on potentially crucial information about race-distance running, as that session is when the teams do their race simulations.

Tyre degradation is expected to be high. The high-grip, smooth new track surface, combined with the longest pit lane of the year - Norris jokingly described it as "6km long", cut in half as it is by a building - should in theory lead to a one-stop strategy.

But the high tyre degradation could well push it to a two-stop, and because teams will try to avoid that, Antonelli said, "probably is going to be grandmother driving in the first 10 laps - we saw how steep the degradation can be, especially if you push too early".

In Norris' favour is that overtaking is expected to be especially difficult.

The straights are short, and some of the corner entries, which combine braking and turning, mean, as Verstappen put it, "there are no corners where you can pass".

The drivers generally liked the challenge of the new track, Norris described it as "a little bit of everything".

But all agreed on the fact that the corner entries need to be changed to facilitate racing.

Verstappen, who qualified third, said: "You can't overtake. So, in some places, the braking zones, like, they need to learn that it should never be that you have to steer, that you have to combine under braking, because it doesn't allow any kind of overtaking."

Antonelli said: "It's going to be tight. I spent two laps behind the Williams, trying to painfully get past. But it's just really difficult.

"And when you're behind, it's tough. Yeah, the only thing you can do is try to put pressure on the car in front, trying to make them do mistakes or make them deg a bit more."

The difficulty in overtaking is what makes this a real opportunity for Norris to take a third win of the season, even if the McLaren is not the fastest car.

As he put it: "It's a long race, it's a new track. You've got to know what corners to push, what corners not to push, all of these different things, what the battery's then going to do.

"There's a lot of stuff that I've got to spend my time doing tonight. So, it's probably going to be a late one to try and get ahead of the game in some sorts. But the main part of the job was done today, so that's the bit I'm most happy about."

title: More dropped points at Anfield - is it too early for Liverpool to worry?
description: Liverpool have failed to win either of their first two Premier League games at Anfield. But is it too early to worry?
fullText:
Two Premier League matches at Anfield. Two draws.

For just the third time in 63 years, Liverpool have failed to win both of their opening home games of a league season - not exactly the flying start new boss Andoni Iraola would have been dreaming of.

After such an encouraging midweek performance against Atletico Madrid in the Champions League, full of urgency, Saturday's goalless draw against Fulham was a flat follow-up, especially with the Cottagers lacking in confidence and having conceded seven goals in their first three league games.

The Reds looked physically and mentally tired and, to put it bluntly, like an entirely different team to the one that won against a Diego Simeone side that made it to the Champions League semi-finals last season.

On the first real look at how Iraola's style will cope with two games a week, this was certainly not what the Liverpool head coach, nor the Anfield crowd, would have wanted to see.

Former boss Jurgen Klopp would often speak about recognising his team based on their identity and intensity rather than just their colours and judging by Iraola's words since he took over, the Spaniard wants the same too.

Iraola said: "What was lacking was quite clear, it is the first game we had problems to create chances and score goals and make the difference offensively, and that is the main reason we couldn't create chances."

His side are still unbeaten and it is hardly a crisis, but he will look at a return of six points from their first four Premier League games as disappointing, particularly by dropping four points at home to Nottingham Forest and Fulham, with another draw coming at Newcastle and their sole success at Ipswich.

Keeper Alisson told Sky Sports: "We are not happy at all with the draw. It is not something that should happen with Liverpool. To be unbeaten, but with three draws, is not something to celebrate too much with this shirt.

"If we want to do something special [this season] we have to cope with playing a game Wednesday, Saturday and then Tuesday.

"We need to have the right mental state and that was not the case from what we showed. Inside we have it, but we have to just put it out and put more energy on the pitch."

The £364m attacking trio of Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz started together for the first time in a league game and although Liverpool had decent chances, they created nowhere near enough.

Isak's 16 touches in 90 minutes was the second fewest for an outfield Reds player on record, having had the fewest (14) against Forest a fortnight ago.

German Wirtz looked a shadow of the player who was terrific in midweek against Atleti and while Barcola and Isak had a few encouraging moments, that is a partnership that will take time to develop.

"Bradley is one we are building up physically with games and the games will give him the condition we want," Iraola told Match of the Day.

"But it is not just Bradley, we lack the freshness. I only remember one clear chance [for Fulham] and we kept the structure but offensively we need to do much better."

Frustrated Liverpool held as Fulham pick up first point

Before the game against Atletico Madrid, Iraola was asked about how he sought to strike the right balance, with the intensity levels he craves and such a busy schedule.

His response was he didn't want his players to save energy because they had another game in three days.

"You play 55 minutes for me and you are dead and ask for a sub, then perfect," said Iraola. "We have a top-level 55 minutes and then a top-level 35 minutes."

Despite sending on Milos Kerkez, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister, Rio Ngumoha and Jeremie Frimpong, Liverpool showed little improvement.

Iraola admitted: "The players were tired and there is a lack of freshness - we cannot hide it. This is the worst turnaround in terms of 60 or 70 hours [since the last game], but this is going to happen in the season and we have to adapt and it is these kind of games that you need to win sometimes with a set-play or a moment of brilliance."

It is still early, but already there is a realisation from Iraola and his players that when they have such short turnarounds between games, perhaps it is a case of adapting and finding ways to get a result.

With at least seven more Champions League games to follow and a Carabao Cup tie at home to Tottenham on Tuesday, Liverpool must adapt sooner rather than later as the fixture list cranks up if they are to show they can challenge for honours this season.

title: England chasing the rainbow with more questions than answers
description: Are England a better team in September than in June? BBC cricket correspondent Stephan Shemilt discusses the positives and negatives of the Test summer and what the next period may bring.
fullText:
It is 2026 and Joe Root is again England Test captain and Kevin Pietersen is back in the fold.

For those two things to be the new normal says plenty about the upheaval in one of the most turbulent summers in English cricket's recent history.

The debate as to whether there should have been alterations to the leadership after the Ashes has become a moot point, because England have nevertheless ended in a post-Bazball era.

Has the lack of change in the spring led to a wasted summer? Try telling any of Jordan Cox, Emilio Gay or Dan Lawrence that the summer has been wasted. Or a resurgent Ollie Robinson. Or Root, who had to rummage around his garage to dig out his old captain's blazer.

Are England a better team in September than they were in June? It is hard to argue that a team that has lost Ben Stokes has improved, though that should take nothing away from all the good things England have done in the 3-0 series sweep of Pakistan.

It is not a criticism of Stokes to say his personality dominated the England team he led. By the end of his reign, England were characterised by what Stokes said and did.

Naturally, England are different under Root, a different personality to Stokes.

Until the third evening of the third Test at Edgbaston, most of those differences seemed positive. There had been a calmness about England's demeanour, perhaps because they had not been tested to that point.

That calmness eroded with every swing of Razaullah's blade. Two hours of chaos frazzled England and exposed old doubts from Root's first spell as captain. The skipper himself felt it necessary to duck off the field. Stokes rarely lost control in such a fashion.

Even after such a bruising session, there were some small positives. Stand-in coach Marcus Trescothick was happy to admit his disappointment at what had transpired, a shift in tone from the Kool Aid messaging of the Bazball boys.

In reality, we are ending the summer with no clear knowledge of how good this England team is, following a pattern of years gone by: the drawn Ashes in 2023, a shock defeat by Sri Lanka at The Oval at the end of 2024 and the failure to win the final Test against India last year.

And that is the ultimate frustration of England's Test performances in the four-plus years that Rob Key has been director of cricket.

When the defining series have rolled around, England have not won them. In between those big challenges there have been more questions than answers. The brass ring always remains just out of reach, always searching for the pot of gold at the end of the rainbow.

England in better place than start of summer - Root

Who has given selectors food for thought? England-Pakistan player ratings

TMS podcast: Cox and Root guide England to clean sweep

For now, England have a blossoming four-man pace quartet that has drawn comparisons with the famous Ashes winners of 2005.

Robinson has ruled England's summer, taking his 28 wickets at an average of 9.32; the sort of statistics in keeping with Test cricket from before World War I.

With Jofra Archer, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson bringing the pace, England have a Swiss army knife of an attack, albeit lacking a left-armer.

Still, England are only one injury away from some inexperienced reserves. Sam Cook, Sonny Baker, Matthew Fisher and Henry Crocombe have four caps between them. Brydon Carse is available, though it remains to be seen if England will take him on tour while the Derby incident is still under investigation. Perhaps the in-form Olly Stone is due a recall.

The challenge for England is to find the right blend to suit the winter. The four seamers could operate in South Africa and the one-off pink-ball 150th anniversary Test in Melbourne, but the two matches in Bangladesh in February will demand a change in formation.

Despite the burning summer, spin has become a redundant weapon. The list of candidates to play in Bangladesh is long because there is no outstanding one among them.

Shoaib Bashir, Jack Leach, Dom Bess, Will Jacks, James Coles, Mason Crane, Liam Patterson-White, Calvin Harrison and Jack Carson may all think they have a shout of being on the plane.

The incumbent is Dan Lawrence, who has not had many opportunities to show the value of his part-time off-breaks.

Lawrence's bowling gives him an advantage when Jacob Bethell returns from a knee injury, probably leaving a choice between Jordan Cox and Emilio Gay for the first Test in South Africa in December.

Both men have made three half-centuries in their first summers as Test batters. Cox is extremely highly rated by the England management, who must decide how much weight to put on Gay's skill as a specialist opener.

The top of the order has emerged as England's biggest batting concern. Ben Duckett made the only century of the summer, yet averages 23 since the beginning of the Ashes.

Gay's average in his six Tests is below 25 and his frustration at his second-innings dismissal against Pakistan came out with a swish of his bat towards the stumps. His running between the wickets is jittery and he is rarely placed in an important position in the field.

Of all the issues around the batting, England need Root to rediscover his best. The captain ends the summer without a hundred for the first time since 2019 and with his lowest average in a home season since the same year.

This time last year, it was full steam ahead in the pursuit of India great Sachin Tendulkar. Now, the 1,643 runs to catch the Little Master look a little further away. The smart money will be on Root to come out of his funk, rather than this being the start of a late-career decline.

Root will meet incoming coach Stephen Fleming in the coming days to plot the route forward.

Along with Key - the great survivor of England's chaotic summer - the trio will look for a way to win the marquee series, to claim the major prizes on offer in the months ahead: in South Africa this winter, the Ashes next summer, in India in early 2028.

And this is where England find themselves yet again, with judgement reserved until biggest challenges.

Still grasping for the brass ring, still chasing the pot of gold.

title: Missouri's Eli Drinkwitz tried to embarrass Kansas with late score, bemoans Jayhawks making rivalry about Civil War
description: Drinkwitz doesn't see the point of the historic series continuing if Kansas, in his eyes, keeps turning it deeper than it needs to be on the gridiron.
fullText:
Eli Drinkwitz doesn't usually mince words. While mostly affable, the Missouri head coach doesn't always He's not to afraid to say how he feels.

He certainly didn't pull any punches after his No. 23 Tigers squad humbled Kansas on the road Friday night in the latest iteration of the schools' "Border Showdown." Missouri (2-0) handed the Jayhawks (1-1) a 38-21 defeat that could have looked even more lopsided had a head-turning shot to the end zone not fallen incomplete in the game's waning moments at David Booth Kansas Memorial Stadium in Lawrence.

That potential death knell resulted from Drinkwitz's frustration toward Kansas and the way the Jayhawks brazenly approached the programs' longstanding yet complicated rivalry in the lead-up to the matchup.

Kansas leaned into the Civil War history between the two states, posting a pregame hype video framed as "heroes vs. villains" with the social media caption, "It is that deep." Drinkwitz wasn't amused and fundamentally disagreed.

"I'm just glad this whole right vs. wrong bullcrap that was started just got settled on a football field...I get there's a past to it but why are we stirring that bullcrap up."

Eli Drinkwitz shares his thoughts on "the turn" the Mizzou/KU rivalry took this week. pic.twitter.com/g5fmQypJx6

"I get there's a past to it, but why are we stirring that bull crap up? It's 9/11," Drinkwitz said postgame on Friday, the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks.

"This country needs unity now more than ever. And I was embarrassed for 'em, to be honest."

Drinkwitz added, in reference to Missouri's pass that could have ran up the score with less than 30 seconds left: "And that's why I tried to embarrass them at the end."

Now in his seventh season at the helm of the Tigers, Drinkwitz expressed disappointment in "the turn" the fabled series between the neighboring programs took.

"I thought that was uncalled for," he said. "And this is about two teams playing football, and especially on 9/11 when we need more unity now than ever before — to be putting some stuff on your screen, celebrating ... I mean, everybody's got complicated pasts.

"To make that an icon was bizarre to me. So I'm just glad that this whole right-versus-wrong bull crap that was started just got settled on a football field because it's a football game. It's a football game. It's an American football game that people love to come watch and cheer for their teams.

"It's not any deeper than that."

It is that deep. pic.twitter.com/4BEcdbLv7S

Kansas' aforementioned video, which was narrated by Jayhawks alum and former NFL defensive lineman Gilbert Brown, describes the "Border Showdown" like this:

"It's fueled by hatred passed down through generations," Brown said of the rivalry. "Our roots reach back to the Civil War when blood was spilled over what you believed in and which side you stood on. There are heroes and villains. Only allegiance decides their legacy. There's right and wrong. There's Kansas and Missouri."

Only the 1918 Spanish flu pandemic got in the way of Kansas and Missouri facing off on the gridiron between 1891 to 2011. For more than a century, their head-to-head was a staple in the college football landscape. But in 2012, Missouri left the Big 12 for the SEC, and the rivalry went dormant. Its 14-year hiatus ended last season, with the Tigers outlasting the Jayhawks in Columbia, Missouri.

Missouri leads the all-time series 59-54-9, according to Winsipedia, although the all-time record is a debate subject as well.

As Drinkwitz briefly conceded, "there's a past to" the series. The teams' nicknames come from the Civil War era. And the regional dispute can be traced back to the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, which allowed the two then-territories to vote on their status as free or slave states when they joined the Union. Conflict ensued on the border of Kansas and Missouri — a slave state at the time — as pro-slavery and anti-slavery forces clashed.

That period of violent guerrilla warfare is known as "Bleeding Kansas." It served as a precursor to the Civil War.

"I don't really care if it continues or not," Drinkwitz said, when asked about the football rivalry, which isn't scheduled to pick back up again until 2031.

"I mean, if they're going to be weird about it, then what's the point? If they want to have a football game and play a football game and have a great rivalry on the border, then awesome, let's do it. But if we want to make it deeper than that, man, we left Kansas bleeding again, so call it good."

Missouri broke open Friday's game in the second half, converting a pair of Robert Woodyard Jr. takeaways into touchdowns.

The game was the series' first in Kansas since 2005. It nearly ended with one more Tigers touchdown.

"I mean, I didn't want to score too bad, or I'd have called timeouts and tried," Drinkwitz said postgame after being asked how badly he wanted to score late.

"But I just wanted to — I mean, we didn't think we were going to throw that in the end zone, but I just wanted to let them know, like, 'Dude, what are y'all doing?' This is a football game. It shouldn't be bigger than that."

title: Cleveland Browns DC Mike Rutenberg: ‘We’re arriving with bad intentions’
description: Cleveland new man in charge of the defense has a clear idea of what he wants from his side of the ball.
fullText:
The Cleveland Browns will sport a new defensive look when they take the field on Sunday for their Week 1 game against the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Some of those changes are by design: defensive end Jared Verse replaces Myles Garrett, linebacker Quincy Williams replaces Devin Bush, and defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg takes over for Jim Schwartz.

There were some unexpected changes, however, most notably along the defensive line, after defensive end Alex Wright, who was expected to be a starter, was lost for the season to a torn Achilles tendon.

That led general manager Andrew Berry to bring in veterans Sam Williams and Derek Barnett, and Rutenberg to experiment with Michael Hall Jr. at defensive end.

Rutenberg had his weekly press conference on Thursday and addressed several topics. Here are four takeaways from what he had to say.

There are no bigger shoes to fill for a defensive player than those of Myles Garrett, who picked up his second Defensive Player of the Year Award in 2025 after bagging an NFL-record 23 sacks.

Garrett is now with the Los Angeles Rams, while Verse is in Cleveland and bringing his own style to the defense, according to Rutenberg:

"(Jared's) such a unique guy. He's really like a unicorn in that he sets a standard with his play style and who he is. Really, what we saw early is what we continue to get. He sets that standard from the jump, in meetings, great questions, great insight. And then on the practice field, his standard of not only performance but style, and how hard he plays, has been the same every day. It's really cool to see."

Adding veterans is nice, especially for a team that is in the second year of a youth movement, but adding them so close to the start of the season is not always ideal. Especially with everyone on the defense already working with a new defensive coordinator and not necessarily able to quickly bring the new guys up to speed.

But so far everything has gone smoothly with Barnett and Williams, according to Rutenberg:

"It's awesome to get new guys. The nature of this league is that you get new players, and those guys have worked as hard as you could possibly imagine. They've worked their butts off. Derek's obviously been in it. Sam's had experience in it. Those guys are pros, man. They approach it the right way. We've got a great defensive line coaching staff, starting with Jacques (Cesaire), Ralph (Street), Laroy (Reynolds), Shaq (Wilson), and together they're preparing really hard. It's really cool to see."

finding a way to win on defense@GetSpectrum | #DawgPound pic.twitter.com/pREF2cg2NZ

All through training camp and the preseason, Rutenberg has talked about how "the ball is oxygen," and the defense needs it to survive. He also wants his defense to have a very particular mindset when it takes the field:

"When the ball is thrown, we're arriving with bad intentions. We're built off that. We choose violence in everything we do, and it doesn't have to be a tackle; ball's in the air, we're knocking it out. That's what we're built off. We do our job so my brother can do his; I do mine and a little bit more. And our guys have done that. They do it in practice; they do it in walk-through. It's awesome to see.

"I'm excited to watch us play as hard as possible. I can't wait just to watch us celebrate together. I can't wait to see our preparation hopefully come to life. We're built off violence, and that's what we're looking for in every play."

Far too often, fans and media focus on sacks and turnovers as the only sign that a defense is successful. Those are fun, no doubt, but pressuring a quarterback into a bad throw is just as helpful. And turnovers are not something that a defense can control.

For Rutenberg, however, there is only one clear goal:

"Win. Win. I want to help the Browns win. I learned that from Jeff Ulbrich, man. Raheem Morris used to say, 'help the team win on defense. Find a way to help the team win on defense.' It's a team game; we're a team staff, Browns helping Browns, man. I want to help this team win."

title: New York Mets Suddenly Announce Bad Injury News on 21-Year-Old Top Prospect
description: On Friday, the New York Mets lost the first game of their series to the New York Yankees by a 6-4 final score.The National League East club plays the second game of their series against the Yankees on Saturday and will be aiming to get back in the win column.Now, as the Mets prepare for […] The post New York Mets Suddenly Announce Bad Injury News on 21-Year-Old Top Prospect appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
On Friday, the New York Mets lost the first game of their series to the New York Yankees by a 6-4 final score.

The National League East club plays the second game of their series against the Yankees on Saturday and will be aiming to get back in the win column.

Now, as the Mets prepare for their upcoming game against the Yankees, they have announced some rough news with one of their top pitching prospects.

Gary Gill Hill has been placed on the seven-day injured list, as reported by MiLB.com's official transaction tracker.

Gill Hill being placed on the injured list comes less than a week after he was called up to Triple-A Syracuse from Double-A Binghamton. With that, this development is certainly tough news for the 21-year-old.

Gill Hill is one of the top prospects in the Mets' system. MiLB.com currently has him ranked as New York's fourth-best pitching prospect, so he undoubtedly has good upside. Due to this, it is certainly tough to see him being placed on the injured list so soon after receiving a call-up.

Gill Hill was acquired by the Mets ahead of the 2026 MLB Trade Deadline in the deal that sent Freddy Peralta to the Tampa Bay Rays.

In 26 minor league games split between High-A, Double-A, and Triple-A this season, Gill Hill has a 9-3 record, a 4.25 ERA, and 119 strikeouts. Overall, the young pitcher has been showing promise, and he will be looking to continue to do so once he gets back on the mound.

title: Lions restructure contracts of two stars. What it means
description: Penei Sewell and Amon-Ra St. Brown both got their contracts restructured ahead of Week 1. Could more money be on the way>
fullText:
Some members of the Detroit Lions are looking well beyond Week 1.

On Sept. 12, Lions brass restructured the contracts of two of their star offensive players: wide receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown and right tackle Penei Sewell, according to Spotrac.

The conversion of their base salaries into signing bonuses frees up cap space for the Lions in the immediate, pushing their available cap number to roughly $38 million entering Week 1. That number is good for the second-most cap space in the NFL entering Week 1, sitting behind the San Francisco 49ers.

It's a pair of eyebrow-raising moves, but some that make sense given the Lions' current cap and contract situation, including a pair of their own. Here's what to know:

Contract restructurings are a common part of NFL bookkeeping. Converting a player's base salary into a signing bonus frees up cap space, allowing a team some breathing room to add more money to their cap situation.

There are a few reasons why the Lions may have decided to do it ahead of Week 1.

The Lions have a few players expected to hit free agency come 2027, including tight end Sam LaPorta and safety Brian Branch. It's a possibility that the newly found cap space could be allocated to new contracts keep the two difference-makers in Lions uniforms. Lions GM Brad Holmes has expressed interest in wanting to keep both around this offseason, so talks may have at least happened with both players.

The only and minor snag: Both LaPorta and Branch are rehabbing from injuries as the season gets underway. Branch (PUP list) will miss at minimum the first four games of the season as he recovers from a torn Achilles, while LaPorta is expected to play Week 1 after suffering a hip injury during the preseason. Those injuries may not preclude the Lions' front office from extension talks, but they may want to see both players back in the mix before handing out big-money deals.

Less likely, but still possible. Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Joey Porter Jr. is currently seeking a new contract, which may lead to his exit from Pittsburgh if a deal doesn't come to pass. The Lions have newfound cap space that could allow a new contract to an incoming player. That all could lead to Detroit wanting to upgrade at the position. That said, a trade at this point in the season would be unlikely,

Other names may surface over the coming months leading to the 2026 trade deadline, set for Tuesday, Nov. 10. at 4 p.m. ET.

The Lions could also opt to roll the cap space over into the 2027 offseason. That will give them some extra cash to either dole out for extensions or prep for free agency signings.

The Lions currently hold $38.205 million in cap room, according to OverTheCap. That ranks second in the NFL behind the 49ers, who hold $45.5 million in cap space entering Week 1.
